extracted.intended_audience: vehicle manufacturers, vehicle safety suppliers, test laboratories, and other stakeholders involved in FMVSS No. 210 anchorage strength testing and certification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for evaluating and implementing the Force Application Device (FAD) and the existing body blocks for FMVSS No. 210 anchorage strength compliance testing, including repeatability, equivalence, placement zones, costs, and incorporation by reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatability of seating procedure (FAD positioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess consistency of the FAD seating procedure across technicians and vehicle types (multiple positionings by different technicians; measurement of FAD location).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Karco assessed consistency by having different technicians position the FAD multiple times in nine different vehicles and using a Faro Arm to record seven points on the FAD. Of 27 positionings (3 technicians × 9 vehicles), the average variance for positioning the FAD was less than 1/4 inch; NHTSA considers this variability acceptable and within the same range as FMVSS No. 208's 12.7 mm (1/2 inch) tolerance for the H-point. Note that the seating results were based on three points of the FAD surface, not just one point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatability of forces applied to anchorages
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether forces applied to seat belt anchorages using the FAD are consistent and repeatable over repeated trials on the same seat and vehicle body design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA used three methodologies — coefficient of variation, a general linear model, and a mixed model — across 16 data channels. The coefficient of variation showed most channels rated 'excellent', with one 'good' and one 'acceptable' (the acceptable channel had large measurement error relative to a small mean magnitude). The general linear and mixed models indicated forces tend to be consistent with no statistically significant differences across tests. Use of multiple statistical analyses is recommended to assess repeatability; pay attention to channels with high relative measurement error and the scale of mean values relative to test loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence to existing body blocks (test stringency and compliance outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether use of the FAD would affect the stringency of the anchorage strength test or the likelihood of a vehicle meeting FMVSS No. 210 requirements compared to current body blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA's indicant testing showed vehicles that met anchorage strength requirements using body blocks also met requirements using the FAD. Although load distribution and force vectors may differ (e.g., FAD produced lower outboard shoulder and d-ring forces and higher outboard lap forces on average), the total load on the seat belt assembly anchorages was the same and indicant test data showed equivalent performance. Where differences in load vectors exist, consider whether total load and ultimate pass/fail outcome remain unaffected; further testing across vehicle/seat types is appropriate if commenters or manufacturers raise concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to heavy-duty vehicles and unique seating systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the FAD performs equivalently in medium- and heavy-duty vehicles (which may have unique seating, tethers, air suspension seats, larger cabs, upright seating, and other configurations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA conducted additional indicant tests on heavy-duty buses (GVWR >10,000 lb) including air suspension and pedestal seats; anchorages of all tested seats met FMVSS No. 210 requirements when tested with the FAD. Manufacturers raised concerns about coverage across the wide range of heavy-duty vehicle designs; if coverage is incomplete for a manufacturer's vehicles, NHTSA retained the option for manufacturers to certify using body blocks. When assessing applicability, consider representative testing across vehicle categories and seat/anchorage types and document limitations or exemptions if certain classes (e.g., highly customized heavy trucks) are not covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder access and familiarity with test device
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure manufacturers and test labs have timely access to FAD design information and devices to fabricate, evaluate, and incorporate into their testing programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA docketed FAD design drawings and made 3D design drawings available upon request; NHTSA will make agency FADs available to manufacturers or test labs upon request. Comments suggested reopening the comment period, round-robin testing, and technical workshops; NHTSA must summarize incorporated-by-reference material in the preamble and provide reasonable means to access it (e.g., Regulations.gov, phone, inspection at DOT Docket). Consider allowing manufacturers to continue certifying with body blocks while gaining experience with FADs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing costs and cost-effectiveness (purchase, setup, and amortization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate upfront and ongoing costs of acquiring and using FADs (purchase price, number required, time savings, and impacts on small-volume manufacturers), and consider potential cost savings in labor/time per test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NPRM estimated each FAD ~ $8,000 and an assumed purchase of two FAD1s and three FAD2s (~$40,000). Karco reported installation time savings (6.75 minutes per seating position) and the NPRM estimated labor savings of $18.75 per vehicle test and 5 minutes saved per seat installation. NHTSA notes useful life likely measured in decades and costs can be amortized; small-volume manufacturers may contract out testing or buy shared FADs (e.g., industry association purchase). Consider re-certification and equivalency testing costs: industry estimates for equivalency evaluation/destructive tests ranged broadly (e.g., $20k–$670k) and may drive decisions about allowing both devices as certification options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential re-certification costs and manufacturer burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether adopting the FAD would force manufacturers to re-test or re-certify vehicles previously certified with body blocks, and the associated financial burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some manufacturers expressed that they would need extensive equivalency or re-testing to confirm continued compliance, with cost estimates up to hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on vehicle variety. NHTSA responded by retaining the body block certification option and modifying the body block procedure; agencies should evaluate whether final rules require re-certification or provide an option to defer to existing methods to mitigate undue burden on small-volume manufacturers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference and public availability of technical drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: When material (e.g., FAD drawing packages) is incorporated by reference in a final rule, summarize the material in the preamble and ensure it is reasonably available to interested parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA incorporated 'Drawing Package for the Force Application Device 1 (FAD1), April 9, 2024' and 'Drawing Package for the Force Application Device 2, April 9, 2024,' placed copies in the docket, and provided multiple access methods (Regulations.gov, telephone, DOT Docket Operations). Agencies must comply with 1 CFR 51.5(b) requirements when incorporating materials by reference and document availability methods in the rule preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and refinement of body blocks (zones for placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain body blocks as an option and refine the test procedure to specify zones within which the body blocks will be placed at preload to provide manufacturers notice and improve repeatability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In response to the Chrysler decision, NHTSA will amend the body block test procedure to clearly specify placement of the body blocks at preload using defined zones (similar concept to FMVSS No. 222). The zones limit positioning to improve repeatability; implementation may add complexity but is practicable with positioning aids. Manufacturers may choose between FAD and body blocks for certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference point for determining zone locations (use SgRP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify zone boundaries relative to an objective reference point for repeatable placement of body blocks; choose SgRP over TBAH or H-point for FMVSS No. 210.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA decided to base zones on the SgRP (a manufacturer-determined design point near the hip of a 50th percentile adult male) rather than the TBAH or H-point because SgRP provides a more adequate torso location and avoids variability associated with TBAH in non-school-bus vehicles. Commenters had argued for TBAH or H-point; NHTSA explains trade-offs and implementation considerations (e.g., if H-point not provided, agency responsibility to determine it leads to variability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods and aids to assist body block positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify practical methods to assist in positioning body blocks within specified zones to improve repeatability and practicability of test setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positioning aids can include lasers, Faro Arm measurements, and other alignment tools; for vehicles with accessibility constraints, sections of the vehicle can be removed to improve access and visibility. NHTSA's testing indicated these methods can be readily implemented by test laboratories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of seat and seat belt design factors affecting block placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for seat cushion contours, bolster shape, seat back size, air suspension seats, tethers, and other seat/seat belt design factors that affect preload position of body blocks and the practicability of zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted body block fit and preload position depend on seat and belt designs; IMMI, JCI, EMA, Alliance, and Global flagged variations across seats and heavy-truck designs. NHTSA considered these factors during zone development and concluded the zone concept addresses them, but implementation must recognize seats where blocks may not fit well or where zones may need special handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance benchmarks and acceptability thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use empirical tolerance comparisons to determine acceptability of variability in device placement or measurement error (e.g., compare FAD placement variance to established H-point tolerances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHTSA compared observed average FAD positioning variance (<1/4 inch) to FMVSS No. 208's H-point tolerance of 12.7 mm (1/2 inch) to justify acceptability. For force measurement channels, interpret coefficient of variation ratings (excellent/good/acceptable) in light of absolute mean magnitudes (e.g., small mean values may make relative measurement error appear large but have minor effect on overall results). Use established regulatory tolerances as benchmarks when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of device geometry differences and their impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that the FAD and body blocks have inherently different geometry and articulation, which may change load vectors and distribution though not necessarily the total load or pass/fail outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAD is a hinged two-piece device with restricted relative articulation; the torso body block is supported by the torso belt and current body blocks move independently. These geometry differences can shift loads (e.g., FAD tends to lower outboard shoulder/d-ring forces and raise outboard lap forces). When evaluating equivalence, focus on total load and ultimate compliance outcome rather than expecting identical per-anchor load distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of manufacturer choice to certify with either device
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow manufacturers the option to certify compliance to FMVSS No. 210 using either the refined body block procedure or the FAD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some manufacturers may find the FAD impracticable or face high testing/recertification costs for certain vehicle types, NHTSA decided to retain body blocks and provide manufacturers the ability to choose which device to use for certification. This option mitigates concerns about unfamiliarity, availability, and potential re-certification burdens.
